title: Caravaggio's Matthew
hookLine: a painting of the tax collector at his table with light falling through a window

cards: In a side chapel of San Luigi dei Francesi, a church in Rome, visitors stand in front of one painting and ask each other: which one is he?

Several men sit around a table in a dim room, in the fashionable clothes of the painter's own day: feathered hats, puffed sleeves, a sword. Coins lie on the table. Two figures have just walked in from the right.
One of them lifts his hand and points. A shaft of light cuts across the wall above them. The painter is Caravaggio, and the moment is the calling of Matthew.

teach.b: The Gospel gives this moment a single verse. Matthew is sitting at the custom house, collecting taxes, and Jesus, passing by, says to him, in the Douay-Rheims: "Follow me." And he gets up and follows.
Caravaggio stretches that verse into a whole room. First, the ordinary room. No temple, no clouds, no halo to speak of.
Tax collectors were distrusted in the Gospels, and Caravaggio sets them in what looks like a back office in his own Rome. The call walks into the place where people count money. Second, the hand.
Jesus's hand reaches toward the table, loose, almost lazy. Viewers often notice that it echoes the hand of Adam in Michelangelo's creation scene in the Sistine Chapel.
A call, the painting suggests, is a kind of new creation. Third, the light.

teach.h: THE LIGHT RUNS WITH THE HAND.
teach.b: It comes from behind Jesus, from the upper right, and runs across the wall in the same direction as his hand.
The light points where he points. Fourth, the question. The bearded man at the table gestures, maybe at himself: me?

Or maybe at the young man beside him, slumped over the coins, who won't look up. For a long time viewers took the bearded man for Matthew; some art historians now argue it's the young one. The painting doesn't settle it.
Either way, in Caravaggio's telling, the call lands on someone who hasn't earned it, sitting with his money in a dim room, and the light gets there first.

how: The Calling of Saint Matthew still hangs in the Contarelli Chapel of San Luigi dei Francesi in Rome, where visitors, pilgrims and parishioners stop to look at it before and after Mass.

games.q: you're at your table, counting the day's taxes. a stranger stops, points at you, and says: follow me. what do you do?
o: finish counting, then think about it.
point at the man next to you.
games.why: the Gospel gives it one verse: he arose up and followed him. Caravaggio paints the moment just before.

practice: If you can, find a picture of the Calling of Saint Matthew and let your eyes go where the light goes, then to the hand, then to the faces at the table, one by one. Which one do you take for Matthew?
If you pray, hear the words follow me as spoken to you; if you don't, keep looking, slowly.

wordCard.voice: Caravaggio's Matthew. The Calling of Saint Matthew, painted for a chapel in Rome, where light and a pointing hand find a tax collector at his table.
